hints: Focus on the temperature condition, cold versus hot changes the product of chlorine disproportionation.
In cold alkali, chlorine is both reduced to oxidation state -1 and oxidised only mildly to oxidation state +1.
Match those two oxidation states to chloride and chlorate(I) ions, then check which pair fits.
walkthrough:
**Spot the disproportionation**

Chlorine starts at oxidation state 0 in $\text{Cl}_2$. When it reacts with alkali it is simultaneously reduced and oxidised, so this is disproportionation.

$$\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cl}^- + \text{Cl(+I or +V)}$$

**Remember cold versus hot**

Cold dilute alkali gives a mild oxidation to +1. Hot concentrated alkali gives stronger oxidation to +5. This question says cold, so expect the +1 product.

$$\text{cold: } \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify the anions**

The products are potassium chloride and potassium chlorate(I). The potassium ion $\text{K}^+$ is a spectator, so the anions left in solution are chloride and chlorate(I).

$$\text{anions = } \text{Cl}^- \text{ and } \text{ClO}^-$$

options.A: Correct. Cold aqueous KOH gives $\text{KCl}$ and $\text{KClO}$ plus water. The anions are $\text{Cl}^-$ (oxidation state -1) and $\text{ClO}^-$ (chlorate(I), Cl in +1). This is the classic cold disproportionation.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{ClO}_3^-$ is the pair formed with hot concentrated alkali, not cold. The equation is $3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{OH}^- \rightarrow 5\text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}_3^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This traps students who mix up hot and cold conditions.
options.C: Incorrect. Perchlorate, $\text{ClO}_4^-$ with Cl in +7, is not formed by chlorine with alkali under these conditions. It requires much stronger oxidising conditions. Students sometimes guess it as a further oxidation product.
options.D: Incorrect. Both $\text{ClO}^-$ and $\text{ClO}_3^-$ are oxidised products, but disproportionation must also give the reduced product $\text{Cl}^-$. This option misses chloride and wrongly combines the cold product with the hot product.
